chapterTitle: Working with Data: CRUD Operations (Update & Delete) and Data Types
aiGenerationNote:
Produce a 15-minute live coding video demonstrating update and delete operations in `mongosh`. Start by updating a single document using `$set` and `$inc`. Then show how to use `$push` and `$pull` for array manipulations. Illustrate the difference between `updateOne()` and `updateMany()`, emphasizing the caution needed for `updateMany()`. Follow with `replaceOne()`, clearly showing how it replaces the entire document. Conclude with `deleteOne()` and `deleteMany()`, including a strong safety warning about `deleteMany({})`. Throughout the video, intersperse explanations of key BSON data types like `ObjectId`, `Date`, `Double`, and `Decimal128` with practical examples of when to use each. Include a 3-question interactive quiz focused on choosing the correct update operator for various scenarios.

screens.title: Updates, Deletes, and BSON Types
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how MongoDB updates and deletes documents and why choosing the right BSON types matters. We'll cover the three update methods — updateOne, updateMany, and replaceOne — and the key update operators you will use every day, such as $set, $inc, $unset, $push, and $pull. You will also learn how deleteOne and deleteMany behave and why deleteMany requires extra caution. Then we shift focus to BSON: ObjectId, number types, Decimal128, Date, arrays, and embedded documents. This matters because the types you choose affect query correctness, indexing behaviour, and numeric precision. For example, using Decimal128 for money avoids rounding errors that doubles can produce. Throughout the chapter you'll practice with concrete mongosh commands and verification steps to build safe, repeatable workflows. By the end you will know how to update a single document, apply bulk changes safely, replace documents when needed, delete with care, and pick BSON types that fit your data and queries.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Safety
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives screen focuses on practice and safety. You will learn verification patterns such as running find() with the same filter before an updateMany or deleteMany, and using small, reversible changes in development before production runs. The hands-on activity in the chapter walks you through updating a single product, incrementing stock across categories, adding array elements, unsetting fields, replacing a document by _id, and both single and bulk deletions. Each exercise includes a verification find() command so you can see exactly which documents were affected. These steps reduce risk when you perform powerful operations. Finally, you will learn a simple rule: replaceOne expects a full document and will remove omitted fields, while updateOne and updateMany expect update operators. That difference is a frequent source of mistakes. Practice these verification steps until they become habit to avoid accidental data loss and ensure your updates reflect the intended model.

keyIdea.title: Safety First
keyIdea.text: Always verify filters with find() and remember replaceOne replaces the full document, while update methods use update operators.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Practice & Safety
Practice & Safety
Verification steps that prevent accidental changes
Verification pattern
  • Run find() with the same filter to preview matched documents before updateMany or deleteMany.
  • Test changes on a non-production copy when possible, or run limited queries first.
  • Remember replaceOne replaces the entire document; include _id or omitted fields will be removed.
  • Use combined update operators to change multiple fields in one updateOne call.
Quick Check
Before a bulk operation, run:
db.products.find({ category: "Peripherals" })
Confirm matched documents, then run the update or delete.

screens.title: Update methods: updateOne, updateMany, replaceOne
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the three primary update methods and their intent. updateOne targets a single document that matches a filter and applies an update document, typically containing update operators. Use it when you want to change specific fields on a single record, for example updating a user's email. updateMany applies the same update document to every document matching the filter. It's useful for bulk adjustments, such as adding a new warranty field for all products in a category or incrementing stock across many items, but it carries risk if your filter is too broad. Always preview matches with find() before running updateMany. replaceOne replaces the entire document that matches the filter with a new document you provide. The _id field must be preserved; otherwise replaceOne will overwrite other fields and remove those you omit. A common mistake is trying to use update operators like $set with replaceOne — replaceOne expects a full document, not operators. In practice, choose updateOne for targeted changes, updateMany for deliberate, tested bulk edits, and replaceOne when you truly intend to rewrite the document structure. Which method to pick depends on whether you need partial field changes or a full replacement.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Update Methods
Definition and intent
Clear definitions help you choose the right method for the task.
updateOne()
Updates a single document that matches the filter using update operators. Use for specific record edits and verify with find() first.
updateMany()
Updates all documents matching the filter. Useful for bulk changes but preview matches beforehand to avoid unintended modification.
replaceOne()
Replaces the entire document with a provided document. Do not use update operators here; omitted fields are removed.
Key Takeaway

Method choice defines whether you alter fields or replace structure. Use replaceOne sparingly and with the document's _id preserved.

Concrete examples
db.products.updateOne(
  { name: "Wireless Mouse" },
  { $set: { price: 29.99, lastUpdated: new Date() } }
);

db.products.updateMany(
  { category: "Peripherals" },
  { $inc: { stock: 5 } }
);

db.products.replaceOne(
  { name: "Mechanical Keyboard" },
  {
    name: "Mechanical Keyboard Pro",
    brand: "Razer",
    price: 129.99,
    stock: 60,
    category: "Gaming Peripherals"
  }
);
Verify each change with db.products.find(filter) to confirm matched documents before and after the operation.

screens.title: updateOne with multiple operators
screens.narratorSegment: In real workflows you'll often need to change multiple fields at once on a single document. updateOne accepts a filter and an update document where you can combine operators. For example, you may want to change a product's price, increment a numeric counter, and add a tag to an array in one call. This reduces round trips and keeps the change atomic for that document. A concrete, chapter-provided example updates a product's price and lastUpdated with $set. You can extend that pattern by adding $inc to decrement or increment stock and $push to append a tag. A common misconception is that update operators mutate nested arrays or fields without initialization; $push will create the array if it doesn't exist, while $inc initializes a missing numeric field to zero before applying the increment. After running updateOne, always run a find() to inspect the single document you modified. This confirms operator behavior and helps detect unexpected removal or type changes. Use this pattern for controlled, multi-field edits to keep your operations precise and efficient. updateOne with multiple operators means combine multiple update operators in one updateone call to make several coherent changes atomically to a single document.. In practical terms, combine $set, $inc and $push to perform several changes in one command. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › updateOne Walkthrough
Code Walkthrough
Multiple operators in a single updateOne
db.products.updateOne(
  { _id: ObjectId("YOUR_PRODUCT_ID_HERE") },
  {
    $set: { price: 34.99, lastUpdated: new Date() },
    $inc: { stock: -1 },
    $push: { tags: "sale" }
  }
);

// Verify
// db.products.find({ _id: ObjectId("YOUR_PRODUCT_ID_HERE") });
  • $set changes or adds fields such as price.
  • $inc adjusts numeric fields; missing numbers initialize to zero first.
  • $push appends to arrays and creates the array if it did not exist.
Concrete scenario
A customer returns an item and you need to lower stock, add a 'restocked' tag, and record the lastUpdated timestamp in one operation.
Key Takeaway

Combining operators in updateOne is efficient and reduces the chance of partial updates across multiple calls. Always verify after the operation.

Common Mistake

Expecting replace semantics when you use replaceOne-like behavior with update operators. Use replaceOne only with a full document, not operators.

screens.title: updateMany: bulk changes and safety checks
screens.narratorSegment: updateMany is powerful because it applies the same update to all documents that match a filter. Use it when you need consistent changes across many records, for example increasing stock for an entire category. But that power requires disciplined safety checks. Start with a find() that uses the intended filter so you can inspect the exact documents that will change. The chapter suggests testing queries in development or using a limited set before applying broad changes. In practice, run db. collection. find(filter). limit(10) to sample matches, then run a complete find to confirm. After you are confident, run updateMany with the update operators you need. Remember that updateMany takes the same update document structure as updateOne, so you can combine $inc, $set, and array operators. A misconception to avoid: updateMany will not implicitly narrow its scope — your filter defines the set precisely. If you accidentally run updateMany({}), it will modify every document in the collection. Always double-check your filter and back up data or test in a non-production environment when possible. updateMany: bulk changes and safety checks means always preview matched documents with find() and test updates in development before running updatemany in production.. In practical terms, preview matches, test on a subset, then apply bulk updates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › updateMany Safety
Safety Process
A four-step pattern to prevent unintended bulk changes.
  1. Preview: Run db.collection.find(filter) to inspect matched documents.
  2. Sample: Use .limit(10) to confirm representative documents.
  3. Test: Run the update on a development copy or narrow filter first.
  4. Execute: Run updateMany only after confirming results and backups.
Example
db.products.find({ category: "Peripherals" }).limit(10)

db.products.updateMany(
  { category: "Peripherals" },
  { $inc: { stock: 5 } }
);
Why previewing matters
Previewing avoids the single-big-mistake scenario such as running updateMany({}) which touches every document. Backups or running updates in non-production are recommended best practices.
Warning

deleteMany({}) and updateMany({}) without filters will affect all documents. Confirm filters and test first.

screens.title: replaceOne vs update (operators)
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing replaceOne with updateOne/updateMany highlights an important modeling concept. replaceOne replaces the entire matched document with the new document you provide. That means any fields not present in the replacement are removed. updateOne and updateMany, by contrast, take an update document that typically contains update operators like $set and $inc to change specific fields while leaving the rest intact. A frequent mistake is attempting to use $set inside replaceOne or expecting replaceOne to merge fields. That won't work — replaceOne expects a full document. Another misconception is that replaceOne preserves all fields except those you list; instead it discards omitted fields. Use replaceOne when you truly want to rewrite the document schema or reset fields, and always ensure the _id remains the same. For partial changes, prefer updateOne or updateMany with operators so you don't accidentally remove important data. When in doubt, preview the result by running a temporary find projection or testing replaceOne in a development copy. replaceOne vs update (operators) means replaceone rewrites the whole document; updates with operators modify only listed fields. use replaceone only when full replacement is intended.. In practical terms, understand the functional difference and common mistakes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › replaceOne vs update
replaceOne
Full replacement of a matched document. _id must be preserved.
db.products.replaceOne(
  { name: "Mechanical Keyboard" },
  {
    name: "Mechanical Keyboard Pro",
    brand: "Razer",
    price: 129.99,
    stock: 60,
    category: "Gaming Peripherals"
  }
);
Omitted fields from the new document are removed from the stored document.
updateOne / updateMany
Partial updates using operators — safer for preserving existing fields.
db.products.updateOne(
  { name: "Wireless Mouse" },
  { $set: { price: 34.99 }, $inc: { stock: -1 } }
);
Use operators to avoid unintentional field removal.
Quick Decision Rule

If you want to change only some fields, use update operators. If you want to rewrite the document exactly, use replaceOne while preserving _id.

screens.title: Update Operators — $set and $inc
screens.narratorSegment: $set and $inc are two of the most commonly used update operators. $set assigns a value to a field. If the field does not exist, $set creates it. This makes $set the safe way to add or change properties without affecting other fields. For numeric adjustments, $inc increments or decrements a numeric field by the given amount. If the field is missing, MongoDB initializes it to zero before applying the increment. An important practical point: combine $set and $inc when you need to change a value and update counters in one call. For example, use $set to change price and $inc to decrement stock when an order is fulfilled. A misconception is to assume $inc will convert strings to numbers; it will not — the field must be numeric or missing. Use these operators to make minimal, predictable changes and always verify with a follow-up find() to confirm the new type and value. These operators keep updates focused and reduce the risk of losing unrelated fields. Update Operators — $set and $inc means $set changes or adds fields; $inc adjusts numeric fields and initializes missing numerics to zero before applying changes.. In practical terms, set field values and adjust numeric fields safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › $set & $inc
$set
Assigns or creates a field with a new value.
db.products.updateOne(
  { name: "Wireless Mouse" },
  { $set: { price: 34.99, warranty: "1 year" } }
);
Use $set to safely add or change properties without altering other fields.
$inc
Increments or decrements numeric fields by a specified value.
db.products.updateMany(
  { category: "Peripherals" },
  { $inc: { stock: 5 } }
);
Missing numeric fields are initialized to zero before applying $inc.
Example Use
Change price and decrement stock in a single update to keep operations atomic for that document.
Misconception
$inc does not convert strings to numbers; ensure the field is numeric or absent before using $inc.

screens.title: Array and field removal operators — $push, $pull, $unset
screens.narratorSegment: $push, $pull and $unset give you precise control over arrays and fields. $push appends a value to an array and will create the array if it doesn't exist, which is handy when adding tags or events. $pull removes all instances of a specified value from an array, useful when you need to remove a tag or value from many documents. $unset deletes a field from a document entirely; provide a field name with any value and MongoDB will remove that field. A typical workflow is to $push a new tag when enabling a feature, $pull a deprecated tag, and $unset temporary or legacy fields you no longer need. A common gotcha is assuming $pull will delete only a single instance; it removes all matching instances in the array. After array operations, inspect the document to confirm the array shape. When designing schemas think about how often you'll add or remove elements and whether embedding arrays fits expected query patterns. These operators let you evolve documents without replacing the entire record. Array and field removal operators — $push, $pull, $unset means $push appends and creates arrays, $pull removes matching items, and $unset deletes a field from a document.. In practical terms, modify arrays and remove fields cleanly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: $push appends and creates arrays, $pull removes matching items, and $unset deletes a field from a document.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Array & Field Operators
Array & Field Operations
Common operations for arrays and removing fields.
$push
Adds an element to an array field; creates the array if missing.
db.products.updateOne(
  { name: "Gaming Monitor" },
  { $push: { tags: "high-refresh" } }
);
$pull
Removes all instances of a value from an array.
db.products.updateOne(
  { name: "Gaming Monitor" },
  { $pull: { tags: "old-tag" } }
);
$unset
Removes a field from a document entirely.
db.products.updateOne(
  { name: "Wireless Mouse" },
  { $unset: { details: "" } }
);
Practical notes
  • $push creates missing arrays; $pull removes all matching values, not just one.
  • $unset removes the field entirely, which may affect projections and indexes.
  • Check post-update documents to ensure arrays and field presence match expectations.

screens.title: Deleting documents with deleteOne and deleteMany
screens.narratorSegment: Deleting data is irreversible unless you have backups, so treat delete operations with care. deleteOne removes at most one document that matches the filter. Use it when you want to remove a specific record, for example a product by name or _id. deleteMany removes all documents that match the filter. This is useful for removing stale data, but it's also the operation most likely to cause catastrophic data loss if misused. The chapter explicitly warns against running deleteMany({}) which deletes every document in the collection. Good practice is to preview with find(), and even run find with the same filter to list documents that will be deleted. In production, consider backing up affected documents before deletion or testing on a staging copy first. After deletion, verify by running the same find() query to ensure no unexpected documents were removed. Deletion should be deliberate, auditable where possible, and always accompanied by verification steps. Deleting documents with deleteOne and deleteMany means use deleteone for targeted removal and deletemany with careful filters and verification to avoid accidental full-collection deletions.. In practical terms, remove single or multiple documents; always confirm matched documents first. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: BSON Data Types and Modeling Choices
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding BSON types is essential for correct queries, indexing, and numeric accuracy. ObjectId is the 12-byte default identifier for _id, containing a timestamp and other pieces to ensure uniqueness across systems. Strings and Booleans function as in JSON. For numbers, MongoDB supports Double, Int32, and Int64; Decimal128 is included for high-precision decimal arithmetic and is recommended for monetary values to avoid floating-point errors. Dates are stored as 64-bit integers representing milliseconds since the UNIX epoch; always use new Date() or ISODate() in mongosh to ensure consistent Date objects rather than strings. Arrays store ordered lists and embedded documents store nested objects, enabling hierarchical structures. A common modeling pitfall is storing numeric IDs as strings or using Double for currency — both can lead to type mismatches or precision loss. Choose types based on how you'll query and calculate values. For example, use Decimal128 for amounts in financial transactions, Date objects for timestamped queries, and ObjectId for unique identifiers so you can reliably join, compare, and index values. BSON Data Types and Modeling Choices means select bson types based on query and precision needs: objectid for identifiers, decimal128 for currency, date for timestamps, arrays/embedded documents for hierarchical data.. In practical terms, objectid, numbers, decimal128, date, arrays and embedded documents. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how MongoDB updates and deletes documents and why choosing the right BSON types matters. We'll cover the three update methods — updateOne, updateMany, and replaceOne — and the key update operators you will use every day, such as $set, $inc, $unset, $push, and $pull. You will also learn how deleteOne and deleteMany behave and why deleteMany requires extra caution. Then we shift focus to BSON: ObjectId, number types, Decimal128, Date, arrays, and embedded documents. This matters because the types you choose affect query correctness, indexing behaviour, and numeric precision. For example, using Decimal128 for money avoids rounding errors that doubles can produce. Throughout the chapter you'll practice with concrete mongosh commands and verification steps to build safe, repeatable workflows. By the end you will know how to update a single document, apply bulk changes safely, replace documents when needed, delete with care, and pick BSON types that fit your data and queries.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to update and delete documents safely and choose BSON types that match your data needs. First, you will perform updates with updateOne, updateMany, and replaceOne, understanding when to alter a subset of fields and when to replace an entire document. Second, you will apply the essential update operators such as $set, $inc, $unset, $push, and $pull for precise field changes, array edits, and numeric adjustments. Third, you will execute deletions using deleteOne and deleteMany while learning verification patterns to avoid accidental data loss. Fourth, you will identify BSON data types including ObjectId, Date, Double/Int32/Int64 and Decimal128, and select them appropriately for indexing, queries, and numeric precision. Together these skills help you manage live collections confidently. Each objective includes hands-on verification steps so you can test queries first, review matched documents with find(), and back up data in a non-production environment before large deletes.

This second objectives screen focuses on practice and safety. You will learn verification patterns such as running find() with the same filter before an updateMany or deleteMany, and using small, reversible changes in development before production runs. The hands-on activity in the chapter walks you through updating a single product, incrementing stock across categories, adding array elements, unsetting fields, replacing a document by _id, and both single and bulk deletions. Each exercise includes a verification find() command so you can see exactly which documents were affected. These steps reduce risk when you perform powerful operations. Finally, you will learn a simple rule: replaceOne expects a full document and will remove omitted fields, while updateOne and updateMany expect update operators. That difference is a frequent source of mistakes. Practice these verification steps until they become habit to avoid accidental data loss and ensure your updates reflect the intended model.

Let's define the three primary update methods and their intent. updateOne targets a single document that matches a filter and applies an update document, typically containing update operators. Use it when you want to change specific fields on a single record, for example updating a user's email. updateMany applies the same update document to every document matching the filter. It's useful for bulk adjustments, such as adding a new warranty field for all products in a category or incrementing stock across many items, but it carries risk if your filter is too broad. Always preview matches with find() before running updateMany. replaceOne replaces the entire document that matches the filter with a new document you provide. The _id field must be preserved; otherwise replaceOne will overwrite other fields and remove those you omit. A common mistake is trying to use update operators like $set with replaceOne — replaceOne expects a full document, not operators. In practice, choose updateOne for targeted changes, updateMany for deliberate, tested bulk edits, and replaceOne when you truly intend to rewrite the document structure. Which method to pick depends on whether you need partial field changes or a full replacement.

In real workflows you'll often need to change multiple fields at once on a single document. updateOne accepts a filter and an update document where you can combine operators. For example, you may want to change a product's price, increment a numeric counter, and add a tag to an array in one call. This reduces round trips and keeps the change atomic for that document. A concrete, chapter-provided example updates a product's price and lastUpdated with $set. You can extend that pattern by adding $inc to decrement or increment stock and $push to append a tag. A common misconception is that update operators mutate nested arrays or fields without initialization; $push will create the array if it doesn't exist, while $inc initializes a missing numeric field to zero before applying the increment. After running updateOne, always run a find() to inspect the single document you modified. This confirms operator behavior and helps detect unexpected removal or type changes. Use this pattern for controlled, multi-field edits to keep your operations precise and efficient. updateOne with multiple operators means combine multiple update operators in one updateone call to make several coherent changes atomically to a single document.. In practical terms, combine $set, $inc and $push to perform several changes in one command. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

updateMany is powerful because it applies the same update to all documents that match a filter. Use it when you need consistent changes across many records, for example increasing stock for an entire category. But that power requires disciplined safety checks. Start with a find() that uses the intended filter so you can inspect the exact documents that will change. The chapter suggests testing queries in development or using a limited set before applying broad changes. In practice, run db. collection. find(filter). limit(10) to sample matches, then run a complete find to confirm. After you are confident, run updateMany with the update operators you need. Remember that updateMany takes the same update document structure as updateOne, so you can combine $inc, $set, and array operators. A misconception to avoid: updateMany will not implicitly narrow its scope — your filter defines the set precisely. If you accidentally run updateMany({}), it will modify every document in the collection. Always double-check your filter and back up data or test in a non-production environment when possible. updateMany: bulk changes and safety checks means always preview matched documents with find() and test updates in development before running updatemany in production.. In practical terms, preview matches, test on a subset, then apply bulk updates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparing replaceOne with updateOne/updateMany highlights an important modeling concept. replaceOne replaces the entire matched document with the new document you provide. That means any fields not present in the replacement are removed. updateOne and updateMany, by contrast, take an update document that typically contains update operators like $set and $inc to change specific fields while leaving the rest intact. A frequent mistake is attempting to use $set inside replaceOne or expecting replaceOne to merge fields. That won't work — replaceOne expects a full document. Another misconception is that replaceOne preserves all fields except those you list; instead it discards omitted fields. Use replaceOne when you truly want to rewrite the document schema or reset fields, and always ensure the _id remains the same. For partial changes, prefer updateOne or updateMany with operators so you don't accidentally remove important data. When in doubt, preview the result by running a temporary find projection or testing replaceOne in a development copy. replaceOne vs update (operators) means replaceone rewrites the whole document; updates with operators modify only listed fields. use replaceone only when full replacement is intended.. In practical terms, understand the functional difference and common mistakes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

$set and $inc are two of the most commonly used update operators. $set assigns a value to a field. If the field does not exist, $set creates it. This makes $set the safe way to add or change properties without affecting other fields. For numeric adjustments, $inc increments or decrements a numeric field by the given amount. If the field is missing, MongoDB initializes it to zero before applying the increment. An important practical point: combine $set and $inc when you need to change a value and update counters in one call. For example, use $set to change price and $inc to decrement stock when an order is fulfilled. A misconception is to assume $inc will convert strings to numbers; it will not — the field must be numeric or missing. Use these operators to make minimal, predictable changes and always verify with a follow-up find() to confirm the new type and value. These operators keep updates focused and reduce the risk of losing unrelated fields. In practical terms, set field values and adjust numeric fields safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Understanding BSON types is essential for correct queries, indexing, and numeric accuracy. ObjectId is the 12-byte default identifier for _id, containing a timestamp and other pieces to ensure uniqueness across systems. Strings and Booleans function as in JSON. For numbers, MongoDB supports Double, Int32, and Int64; Decimal128 is included for high-precision decimal arithmetic and is recommended for monetary values to avoid floating-point errors. Dates are stored as 64-bit integers representing milliseconds since the UNIX epoch; always use new Date() or ISODate() in mongosh to ensure consistent Date objects rather than strings. Arrays store ordered lists and embedded documents store nested objects, enabling hierarchical structures. A common modeling pitfall is storing numeric IDs as strings or using Double for currency — both can lead to type mismatches or precision loss. Choose types based on how you'll query and calculate values. For example, use Decimal128 for amounts in financial transactions, Date objects for timestamped queries, and ObjectId for unique identifiers so you can reliably join, compare, and index values.
